shipping_slice.notes: GDD 4.3 cuts size classes, the compactor and the crane magnet from the semester slice. Inside the slice every piece is one slot, no piece is ever crushed, and no oversized piece can enter a hold. slot_cost_override is the machine-readable form of slots_per_piece: 1, added this revision because the harness was pricing the hold off size_classes.slots_crushed and getting 3.4 pieces per six slots. The oversized entry keeps its complete-catalog cost of 6 because hand_tetherable is false and oversized_reachable is false, so that cost is never exercised in the slice. The size_classes block above is the complete-catalog description the charter requires me to emit verbatim; it is not the slice's slot model. Anything pricing the slice should read base_slots as a count of pieces and should not price the oversized class at all.

debris.notes: A whole bale of shredded multi-layer insulation off a bus wrap — the lightest thing in the envelope, and the cheapest way to meet the fragile flag on your first launch.
Bus panels folded together by the cascade; the commonest thing in the low envelope and the piece a break-even run is built out of.
Half a wing of shattered cells still on its hinge — light for its bulk, and the glass goes if the shield does.
Structural spine off a comms bus, kinked but sound; the first grab that visibly moves the hold-mass dial.
An expended apogee motor, burnt through and empty — dense scrap steel in one tidy slot.
A folded ten-metre reflector rib cage — the magnet skids off it; crane cable only, so the shipping slice sees it and cannot have it.
Gold-plated wire mesh balled up around its former spar; worth real money by mass and it will not survive a hard flare.
A vented nickel-hydrogen pack on its mounting rails — heavy for the low band and the piece that first pushes a starter hold into amber.
A momentum wheel welded solid by its own bearing failure; a whole lot of dense metal in a single slot.
A titanium helium bottle split along its weld — the densest single-slot grab available to a starter hold.
A heat-pipe panel peeling apart at the bondline; light for its span, glass-brittle, and the last fragile piece before the shipping slice gets serious.
The carbon backbone of a full array wing, cells stripped away — the bread-and-butter mid-envelope haul.
An imager tube with its primary mirror starred through; one slot, high value per kilo, and it cannot be crushed at any tier.
A berthing ring sheared off its tunnel — forged alloy, awkward shape, and no argument about whether it is worth the trip.
Four RCS nozzles on a common manifold, valves fused shut; the best mass-per-slot in the middle third.
A crew-module end dome caved in on itself — crane cable only, and a standing advertisement for the hold you cannot afford yet.
A composite-overwrapped bottle blown open at the boss; heavy, sturdy, and a quarter of a starter hold's mass budget on its own.
Navigation optics in a machined housing, baffle crushed — dense, delicate, and the piece that teaches you to deploy the chute early.
A whole attitude-control tray, three wheels still bolted down — a single grab that eats better than a quarter of a starter hold.
A charred fairing tip off an upper stage, its ablator crazed through — ironic cargo, and it burns first when the shield goes.
A flight computer bay cracked open, boards still seated; the richest fragile piece below the top third and a genuine gamble on your flying.
Tungsten-laced shadow shielding off a nuclear tug — the top third's baseline haul, and it doubles your reentry problem on its own.
A precision high-gain reflector, its face split across the rim — enormous value and no tolerance for a late chute.
Molybdenum accelerator grids arced together into a solid brick; one slot, brutal mass, and half durability the whole way down.
Thirty metres of deployable truss, sheared at the root — crane cable only, and the heaviest ordinary object in the envelope.
A platinum-catalysed cell stack off a crewed vehicle, casing scorched through — the top third's honest workhorse.
A vacuum-jacketed helium dewar with its inner vessel collapsed; heavy, fragile, and worth the whole trip if it lands intact.
A regeneratively cooled nozzle peppered by the cascade — the heaviest thing a hand magnet can legally take home.
A crew hatch with its pane starred, hanging just under the module — the last thing you pass on the way to Armstrong's prize, and a real temptation to overload.

Apollo-era service module hanging at the ceiling, older than the cascade and still whole — one slot, roughly double the ship's mass, and the only object in the catalog that degrades pristine to damaged to scrap instead of breaking. fixed_objective true: it is placed at its altitude every campaign and is never drawn from the weighted spawn pool.

revision_notes: Audit finding full_hold_doubles_mass: accepted in full and fixed by rescaling every mass in the catalog. I was wrong last pass to declare the doubling a top-of-band property; the auditor is right that GDD 2.4 speaks about the hold the harness actually loads, which is the shipping slice at starter storage. Every mass_kg outside Armstrong's module is multiplied by an altitude-dependent factor s(h) = 10.3 - 6.6*(h - 50000)/230000 — 10.2x at the floor, 8.2x at the top of the slice, 4.0x at the ceiling — and then rounded to the kilogram. Nothing else moved: no id, altitude, size class, fragile flag, crushable flag, spawn weight or fixed_objective changed anywhere in the file.

Why a declining factor rather than the flat ~5.6x the balancer proposed. A flat 5.6x lands the slice's spawn-weighted hold at 664 kg, a full_hold_mass_ratio of 1.47 — under the 1.5 bound the audit itself quotes, so it fails the check it was meant to fix. I sized the rescale against the GDD's own flown number instead: GDD 2.2 reports a full hold at approximately 1,398 kg. The rescaled slice's spawn-weighted mean hand-tetherable piece is 231.9 kg, so six slots at one piece per slot is 1,391 kg — 0.5% off the document's figure and a ratio of 1.99 against dry_mass_kg 1400. The factor declines with altitude because the floor is where the shortfall was: lifting the floor 10x and the ceiling 4x is what puts the slice's mean where the rule needs it without pushing Armstrong's module out of its position as the heaviest object in the game.

All four readings the audit and the balancer computed now pass, which is the point of sizing it this way rather than to a single number. One slot per piece over the 19 hand-tetherable slice pieces: mean 238.16 kg, hold 1429 kg, ratio 2.02. The same over all 21 slice pieces including the two oversized: mean 269.3 kg, hold 1616 kg, ratio 2.15. Spawn-weighted over the hand-tetherable slice at one slot per piece: 231.9 kg, hold 1391 kg, ratio 1.99. Spawn-weighted at the size_classes crushed slot cost — the reading the harness takes today, before concern 2 is fixed: 152.6 kg per slot, hold 916 kg, ratio 1.65. The lowest is 1.65 and the highest 2.15, so the check holds whichever slot model the harness settles on, and the disagreement between them stops being able to fail the audit on its own.

Balancer concern 2, the slot table being read where shipping_slice.slots_per_piece should be: accepted, and fixed in the only place I am allowed to fix it. The charter requires size_classes emitted as given, so I did not collapse it to 1/1 — instead shipping_slice now carries slot_cost_override {small: 1, medium: 1, oversized: 6} and hold_mass_model as an explicit formula, which is the machine-readable form of the sentence that block already contained. Oversized keeps its complete-catalog cost of 6 because hand_tetherable is false and oversized_reachable is false, so that number is never exercised against a hold. The masses above are authored for one piece per slot; the factor of 2.05 the balancer measured is now a stated override rather than an inference either of us has to make.

Balancer concern 1, floor masses: this is the same concern I declined last pass, and I was wrong to decline it. It is fixed by the rescale above. The argument I made — that a hold filled at the floor is supposed to be a cheap ride home — survives as a statement about value, not mass: the altitude value multiplier still runs 1.0 to 5.5, so a floor hold is still worth a fraction of a top-of-band one. It just is not weightless any more, and it should not have been.

Balancer concern 3, economy.size_class_base_value.oversized being vestigial: agreed, and no catalog change is needed. shipping_slice.oversized_reachable is false and all three oversized pieces are hand_tetherable false, so nothing in the slice can earn that value. Leaving the key in place to satisfy the schema is the right call. Their job — being the piece the magnet visibly refuses — is unaffected by the rescale.

band_summary recomputed from the final array, not carried over. Means are the plain averages of every piece in each third: bottom 1985/11 = 180.45, middle 3671/10 = 367.1, top 7705/9 = 856.11. fragile_fraction is unchanged in all three thirds because no spawn weight was touched: bottom 9/89 = 0.1011, middle 12/69 = 0.1739, top 10/40 = 0.250.
design_notes: The rescale reproduces GDD 2.2's flown reentry table rather than just satisfying the audit, which is the check I used to know the number was right. Peak heat scales close to the square root of total mass across the document's own three points (empty 1400 kg gives 144.7, module 5000 kg gives 268.8 — an exponent of 0.487). The rescaled full hold is 1,391 kg of cargo on a 1,400 kg ship, so 144.7 * sqrt(2791/1400) = 204.3 against the GDD's stated 203.7 for the full hold. The hold was invisible in flight at 3.5%; it is now worth 41% on the peak, which is what the design says it should be worth.

Mass still climbs monotonically with altitude and the shape of the climb is unchanged — every piece kept its position relative to its neighbours, because s(h) is smooth and every mass was multiplied rather than re-authored. The two small inversions that existed before are still there and still deliberate: the delaminated radiator fin at 120,000 m and the cracked deep space dish at 217,500 m each sit slightly under the piece below them, because both are fragile pieces that are light for their span. Adjacent ordinary pairs stay inside about 30% of each other apart from the floor's first step (56 to 81 kg), which is the same 45% step the catalog has always opened with.

The mass gradient compressed from 5.4x to 3.0x, and that is a consequence of the fix rather than a separate decision. Bottom-third hand-tetherable pieces now mean 154.0 kg against the top third's 468.1 kg. The floor could not stay where it was — the doubling rule pins the slice's mean at roughly 232 kg per piece — and the ceiling could not rise proportionally without a top-of-band hold outweighing Armstrong's module. Counting every piece in each third, including the oversized entries and the module, the bottom-to-top factor reads 4.7x. The risk-versus-reward curve the GDD is buying does not live in the mass ratio alone: the altitude value multiplier runs 1.0 to 5.5 over the same span and multiplies on top of it.

Armstrong's module is still the heaviest thing in the game by a clear margin, and the endgame rule still guards the win condition rather than a nose cone. At 3,600 kg it is 6.9x the heaviest hand-tetherable ordinary piece (the engine bell at 523 kg) and 4.3x the heaviest oversized one. More usefully, it outweighs a full six-slot hold of top-of-band hand-tetherable pieces — about 2,809 kg — by 28%, so no legal hold can reach the module's mass and the plunge-infeasibility rule cannot be satisfied by anything the player could carry instead.

One consequence of the rescale that the balancer and the sweep should see before it surprises them. The harness's full hold is the spawn-weighted slice, 1,391 kg, and that plunges from the top of the band at about 204 bar units — comfortably under the ~235 maxed capacity, exactly as GDD 2.2 requires, and nowhere near the 4%-wide coincidence window the document warns against relying on. But a hold filled entirely with top-third pieces is a different object: 2,809 kg, projecting to about 251 bar units, which is above every shield tier. A player who fills six slots at the ceiling will have to fly a braking pass. I think that is the design working — the good stuff fights you, and it fights you on the way down — but it is a new behaviour that follows from raising the masses, it is not something the harness currently flies, and it should be a deliberate call rather than a discovery.

Fragile fractions are spawn-weighted and were recomputed against the final array: bottom 9/89 = 0.1011, middle 12/69 = 0.1739, top 10/40 = 0.250. No weight moved in this revision, so the gradient is the one the last audit accepted. Counted by piece instead, the same thirds read 4/11, 4/10 and 4/9 — almost flat — which is the failure mode the charter names and the reason the weighted figure is the one reported.

The top third's mean_mass_kg of 856.11 is the plain average the charter asks for and it includes Armstrong's module at 3,600 kg. The ordinary-piece figure is 513.1 kg, and the hand-tetherable ordinary figure — the one anything reasoning about hold mass should use — is 468.1 kg. fixed_objective: true marks the module for exactly that filter.

No piece is strictly dominant, and the rescale did not change which trade each piece offers, only its scale. Density and slot cost stay anticorrelated: the smalls (kick motor casing, pressurant sphere, thruster quad, ion grid) buy mass efficiency per slot at the price of raw value, while the mediums pay better per grab and cost four slots the moment the compactor is ever restored to scope. Fragile pieces remain the high-value-per-kilo end of both classes and can never be crushed, so reaching for one is always a bet on the landing.

Every size class and the fragile flag are still met inside the shipping slice, the bottom two thirds. Small, medium and fragile all appear in the first 40 km of the band; the oversized class is met at 86,500 m as a collapsed dish frame the magnet visibly refuses, so the player learns the crane-cable limit as a rule about the tool rather than as a bug.

Altitudes are unchanged: roughly 7 km centres across the full 50,000-280,000 m envelope, deliberately avoiding the Researcher's sample altitudes of 65,000, 115,000 and 215,000 m. The samples are where the sweep measures, and a catalog that clustered there would be reintroducing three discrete bands under a continuous label.
